Instructions

  1. There are 60 single-correct questions: Biology 1–15, Chemistry 16–30, Mathematics 31–45 and Physics 46–60.
  2. Each question has exactly one correct option. Correct: +4; incorrect: -1; unanswered: 0. All questions are available to attempt; there is no best-three-subject scoring rule.
  3. Use 180 minutes. An on-screen non-programmable scientific calculator is part of the 2026 examination conditions; personal calculators are not allowed under that scheme.
  4. Treat stated data and idealisations as exact unless an approximation is explicitly supplied. Log denotes base 10 and ln denotes the natural logarithm.
  5. The review PDF contains the question paper first, followed by a separate answer key and worked solutions. Keep the solutions hidden during a timed attempt.

Fixed authored order. Figures and IDs must remain linked during review.

QUESTION PAPER / B

Biology

Questions 1-15 · 15 questions · 60 marks

Q1+4 / -1
Three preparations are examined. P has a cell wall, cytoplasmic ribosomes and division on a suitable cell-free nutrient medium. Q contains a nucleic-acid genome within a protein coat and multiplies only in host cells. R is a small circular infectious RNA without a protein coat. Which assignment is supported by all the observations?
A) P virus; Q moneran; R viroid
B) P moneran; Q virus; R viroid
C) P moneran; Q viroid; R virus
D) P viroid; Q virus; R moneran
Q2+4 / -1
A flowering plant has alternate leaves and the illustrated bisexual, actinomorphic flower. Five stamens are attached to the united corolla. The two fused carpels form a superior ovary with axile placentation; fruit is a berry or capsule. Which family best matches the combined evidence?
A) Fabaceae
B) Liliaceae
C) Solanaceae
D) Poaceae
Q3+4 / -1
An isolated lysosomal fraction contains a protein-digesting enzyme. An added large protein substrate cannot cross intact lysosomal membranes. Little digestion occurs with intact vesicles in pH 5 buffer; detergent disruption gives strong digestion at pH 5 but little at pH 7. Enzyme amount is unchanged. Which explanation fits both interventions?
A) Membrane sequestration and an acidic activity optimum restrict where digestion occurs
B) The enzyme is absent until detergent synthesises it
C) The substrate is digested only when the lysosomal membrane pumps ATP into it
D) Detergent raises protein concentration equally at both pH values, fully explaining the difference
Q4+4 / -1
In a stipulated respiratory preparation, one glucose completes glycolysis and both pyruvates are oxidised to acetyl-CoA, but acetyl-CoA cannot enter the Krebs cycle. NAD+ is regenerated by an external system that makes no ATP. Count only net substrate-level ATP and CO2 from those completed stages. What are the two yields per glucose?
A) 4 ATP and 2 CO2
B) 2 ATP and 6 CO2
C) 0 ATP and 0 CO2
D) 2 ATP and 2 CO2
Q5+4 / -1
In a simplified blood-antigen model, a recipient's red cells agglutinate with anti-A and anti-B test sera but not anti-D. The recipient already has anti-D antibodies after a previous sensitisation. Donors are D1=A Rh-negative, D2=O Rh-positive and D3=AB Rh-negative. Ignore all non-ABO/Rh antigens. Which packed-red-cell and plasma pairing avoids the stated antigen-antibody conflicts?
A) D2 red cells and D3 plasma
B) D3 red cells and D1 plasma
C) D1 red cells and D3 plasma
D) D1 red cells and D2 plasma
Q6+4 / -1
In an idealised male reproductive preparation, both vasa deferentia are interrupted while testes, their blood supply and accessory glands remain functional. Which observation distinguishes this intervention from removal of the testes?
A) Semen contains no sperm despite maintained testosterone and ongoing sperm formation within the testes
B) No semen is produced because all seminal fluid originates in the testes
C) Testosterone immediately disappears because it normally travels through the vas deferens
D) The urethra cannot carry urine because the vas deferens is its only outlet
Q7+4 / -1
Two candidate donors have identical profiles at every VNTR locus assayed in a DNA-fingerprinting experiment. A trace sample matches that shared profile. With no other identifying evidence, which conclusion is justified?
A) The trace must contain equal DNA amounts from both candidates
B) The trace is compatible with either candidate, so these assayed markers do not identify which one contributed it
C) The candidates must differ at every untested genomic position
D) Matching profiles prove that no mutation ever occurred in either candidate
Q8+4 / -1
Three transmission models are considered: malaria, filariasis and typhoid. An intervention prevents mosquito bites but does not change drinking-water contamination, sanitation or existing infections. Which pair is expected to have reduced new vector-mediated transmission, and why?
A) Malaria and typhoid, because both multiply in mosquito salivary glands
B) Filariasis and typhoid, because both require mosquito entry into the intestine
C) Typhoid alone, because all mosquito-borne infections are bacterial
D) Malaria and filariasis, because both include a mosquito-mediated entry route
Q9+4 / -1
A recombinant bacterium makes a human proinsulin-like precursor but does not remove its connecting C peptide. Separately produced mature A and B chains can be joined with the correct disulfide bonds to give active insulin. Which interpretation best connects the results?
A) A peptide bond joining the mature A and B chains is the missing permanent insulin linkage
B) Bacteria cannot translate any human-derived amino-acid sequence
C) Precursor processing and correct chain assembly are distinct requirements beyond making the initial polypeptide
D) The C peptide must remain in every mature insulin molecule for receptor binding
Q10+4 / -1
A two-age expected-population model starts with 40 juveniles and 80 adults. During each interval, half the initial juveniles survive and become adults; three-quarters of initial adults survive; each initial adult produces b new juveniles that are all present at the next census. In interval 1, 10 adults immigrate and 10 adults emigrate after reproduction. The next census totals 200. With the same b and survival rates but no migration in interval 2, what are b and the expected total at its end?
A) b=1.75; total 260
B) b=1.50; total 240
C) b=1.50; total 300
D) b=1.00; total 200
Q11+4 / -1
Island birds trace to one ancestral lineage but have diversified into several beak forms associated with different foods. In a separate comparison, distantly related mammalian lineages independently evolve similar burrowing body forms. Which interpretation uses ancestry as well as function?
A) The birds illustrate adaptive radiation; the similar burrowing forms illustrate convergence
B) The birds illustrate convergence because all eat; the mammals illustrate one shared recent radiation
C) Both observations prove that useful forms arise by directed mutation in each individual
D) Both comparisons demonstrate identical ancestry because ecological functions match

A respiratory-volume model has tidal volume 500 mL, inspiratory reserve 2000 mL, expiratory reserve 1000 mL and residual volume 1200 mL. What maximum volume can be expired after a maximal inspiration, without including air that remains after maximal expiration?
A) 4700 mL
B) 3000 mL
C) 3500 mL
D) 1700 mL
Q13+4 / -1

A) P cortisol; Q insulin from beta cells
B) P adrenaline; Q insulin from alpha cells
C) P thyroxine; Q glucagon from beta cells
D) P adrenaline; Q glucagon from alpha cells
Q14+4 / -1
A plant cell has completed nuclear division. The figure shows Golgi-derived vesicles gathering between the two nuclei. A treatment now prevents those vesicles from fusing, but leaves the completed chromosome segregation intact. Which immediate outcome is most directly predicted?
A) Two anucleate cells arise by a cleavage furrow
B) The one cell retains two daughter nuclei and fails to build the initial cell plate
C) The two nuclei fuse automatically into a haploid nucleus
D) DNA replication must reverse before cytokinesis can begin
Q15+4 / -1
In a simplified early mammalian-development experiment, preparation X forms a blastocyst with functional trophoblast but loses its inner cell mass before attachment. Preparation Y retains an inner cell mass but its trophoblast cannot adhere to the endometrium. Other required conditions are maintained. Which paired prediction best separates the two lineage roles?
A) X may attach and still form a normal embryo proper; Y implants because trophoblast adhesion is unnecessary after blastocyst formation
B) X cannot attach solely because its inner cell mass is absent; Y's inner cell mass replaces the trophoblast and restores implantation
C) Neither preparation can have reached a blastocyst because either lineage defect necessarily prevents the earlier cleavage divisions
D) X may begin attachment but cannot form a normal embryo proper; Y can form a blastocyst but cannot implant by the specified route

All omitted occupied orbitals are paired. One electron is removed from the highest occupied level of each molecule. Which comparison follows?

B) N2 strengthens while O2 weakens; neither ion has an unpaired electron
C) N2 weakens while O2 strengthens; each ion has one unpaired electron
D) Both bonds weaken and the ions remain as magnetically paired as their neutral molecules

C) The first change oxidises chromium, while the second requires no electrons
D) The first preserves chromium's +6 state; the second accepts six electrons per dichromate ion

D) A van der Waals radius is always a negative distance

WORKED SOLUTIONS / B

Biology

Method, reasoning and common errors

Q1 Biology · medium

Diversity In the Living World / Cellular division and capsid evidence separate a moneran, virus and viroid

Answer: (B) P moneran, Q virus and R viroid.

Why: P has cellular machinery and can divide without a living host, which distinguishes it from the acellular infectious preparations. A nucleic-acid genome enclosed by a protein coat is consistent with a virus in Q. The infectious naked circular RNA in R matches a viroid, whose organisation lacks a viral protein capsid. Host dependence alone would not distinguish Q from R; coat and cellular evidence must be used together.

Why not the others: (A) reverses the cellular and coated acellular preparations. (C) assigns a protein coat to a viroid and removes that defining distinction from the virus. (D) calls a dividing ribosome-containing cell a viroid and an acellular RNA a moneran.

Key point: Combine cellular organisation, independent division and the presence of a capsid when classifying an infectious preparation.

Q2 Biology · medium

Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals / A family assignment combines epipetalous stamens, carpel fusion and fruit type

Answer: (C) Solanaceae.

Why: The combination of a five-parted united calyx and corolla, five epipetalous stamens, and a bicarpellary superior ovary with axile placentation is characteristic of Solanaceae in the standard family description. The berry-or-capsule fruit supports that assignment. A single trait such as a superior ovary is shared by several families, so the linked whorl arrangement and ovule attachment are more informative than that trait alone.

Why not the others: (A) ordinarily has the distinctive papilionaceous organisation, ten stamens and a monocarpellary legume-producing gynoecium. (B) has a trimerous floral organisation and usually six stamens rather than the illustrated pentamerous one. (D) has the reduced grass-flower organisation rather than the stated five-petalled epipetalous flower.

Key point: Identify a family from a correlated suite of floral and fruit characters rather than one shared feature.

Q3 Biology · medium

Cell: Structure And Functions / A substrate-access intervention is distinguished from a lysosomal pH requirement

Answer: (A) Compartmentalisation and acidic conditions restrict digestion.

Why: Before disruption, the externally added substrate is physically separated from the enzyme, even though the surrounding buffer has a favourable pH. Detergent removes that access barrier, revealing substantial activity at pH 5. The weak rate at pH 7 despite equal enzyme amount shows that access alone is insufficient; catalytic groups and structure also depend on an appropriate acidic environment. The two interventions therefore expose different constraints on the same preparation.

Why not the others: (B) contradicts the stated unchanged enzyme amount and gives detergent an unsupported synthetic role. (C) replaces enzyme-substrate access with an unstated ATP-driven mechanism. (D) cannot explain why the disrupted preparations differ when enzyme amount and substrate supply are controlled.

Key point: Separate compartment access from chemical conditions when interpreting an organelle-enzyme assay.

Q4 Biology · medium

Plant Physiology / Respiratory-stage accounting stops at acetyl-CoA despite cofactor recycling

Answer: (D) 2 ATP and 2 CO2.

Given: Glycolysis and two pyruvate-oxidation reactions finish; no Krebs turnover or external ATP formation occurs.

Formula/Principle: Add the stage-specific carbon and substrate-level ATP balances rather than the full aerobic yield.

Step 1: Glycolysis converts one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvates, releases no CO2 and has net ATP yield 4−2=2 ATP.

Step 2: Each pyruvate loses one carbon as CO2 on conversion to a two-carbon acetyl group. Thus n(COX2​)=2(1)=2 molecules per glucose.

Step 3: Krebs-cycle ATP and CO2 are absent because its stated entry step is blocked.

Why: Producing acetyl-CoA is not the same as oxidising its two carbons through the cycle. External NAD+ regeneration allows the named earlier reactions to continue without silently adding oxidative-phosphorylation ATP. This is a defined stage-accounting model, not the total yield of an intact cell oxidising glucose completely.

Why not the others: (A) counts the two glycolytic ATP investments as retained ATP. (B) assigns all six glucose carbons to CO2 despite the retained acetyl groups. (C) assumes the downstream block stops completed upstream reactions even with the supplied cofactor regeneration.

Key point: Reconstruct ATP and carbon outputs only from stages that actually operate.

Q5 Biology · hard

Human Physiology / An antigen assay and sensitisation history constrain two different blood components

Answer: (C) D1 red cells with D3 plasma.

Why: Reaction with both ABO antisera identifies A and B antigens on the recipient's cells, while the negative anti-D test identifies absence of the D antigen. The pre-existing anti-D makes D-positive donor red cells incompatible in this stated model. D1's A-positive, D-negative red cells introduce neither an ABO antigen foreign to this AB recipient nor D. D3's AB plasma lacks the ordinary anti-A and anti-B antibodies that would otherwise attack the recipient's cells. Red-cell and plasma compatibility must be analysed in opposite directions because one supplies antigens and the other supplies antibodies.

Why not the others: (A) introduces D-positive cells into a recipient with anti-D. (B) supplies group-A plasma containing anti-B against the recipient's B-bearing cells. (D) supplies group-O plasma with anti-A and anti-B against the recipient's AB cells.

Key point: In an antigen-antibody model, analyse donor-cell antigens and donor-plasma antibodies separately; actual transfusion practice additionally requires clinical compatibility procedures.

Q6 Biology · medium

Reproduction / A reproductive-duct intervention separates transport, gametogenesis and endocrine function

Answer: (A) Sperm transport is interrupted while testicular functions persist.

Why: The vas deferens carries sperm away from the testis-associated storage and transport pathway. Interrupting that route prevents sperm from reaching the ejaculate, but does not remove the tissue that produces sperm or the Leydig cells that release testosterone into blood. Accessory glands can still contribute seminal secretions. The observation therefore separates transport failure from loss of endocrine and gamete-producing organs.

Why not the others: (B) ignores accessory-gland contributions to seminal fluid. (C) assigns a blood-borne hormone to the sperm duct as its necessary transport route. (D) confuses the reproductive duct connection with the separate bladder-to-urethra urinary route.

Key point: A blocked reproductive transport route need not abolish gamete formation or endocrine secretion.

Q7 Biology · easy

Genetics And Evolution / Identical assayed VNTR profiles limit individual identification without implying a mixture

Answer: (B) Either candidate is compatible with the assayed profile.

Why: A profile is a set of observations at selected variable loci. When both candidates share those observations, matching the trace does not distinguish them within the assay's information. It also does not demonstrate that both contributed DNA, because one donor alone could produce the same result. Broader identity or mutation-history claims require evidence beyond the markers actually measured.

Why not the others: (A) turns compatibility with two sources into proof of a two-source mixture and an unmeasured mixture ratio. (C) infers universal difference at unobserved positions from equality at the observed ones. (D) makes an absolute historical claim that a finite marker panel cannot establish.

Key point: State what a fingerprint can distinguish in the candidate set, not what its name suggests it should identify.

Q8 Biology · medium

Biology In Human Welfare / A vector-exposure control distinguishes protozoan and helminth routes from typhoid ingestion

Answer: (D) Malaria and filariasis.

Why: Malaria and filarial infection are transmitted through mosquito vectors in the standard disease cycles, even though their causative organisms and vector associations differ. Blocking bites interrupts that shared exposure route without directly killing pathogens already inside a host. Typhoid is associated with ingestion of contaminated food or water rather than a required mosquito-bite stage, so the stipulated intervention does not directly remove its route. This prediction concerns new transmission, not an immediate cure or a measured effect size.

Why not the others: (A) wrongly inserts typhoid into a mosquito cycle. (B) again makes typhoid vector-borne and misplaces the mosquito's role. (C) misclassifies the protozoan and helminth infections as bacteria and reverses the route-based prediction.

Key point: Compare the specific life-cycle entry route when predicting an intervention's direct effect.

Q9 Biology · medium

Biotechnology / Proinsulin processing distinguished from expression and disulfide assembly of mature insulin

Answer: (C) Processing and correct assembly matter beyond translation.

Why: Proinsulin contains a connecting segment that is removed during maturation. Mature insulin retains A and B chains linked by the appropriate disulfide arrangement rather than by retaining that C-peptide connector. Producing the precursor therefore does not guarantee producing the mature active molecule. Activity after correct assembly of separately produced chains shows that expression of human-derived chains is possible, while processing and folding remain separate biochemical tasks.

Why not the others: (A) substitutes a permanent interchain peptide connection for the stated mature disulfide linkage. (B) contradicts production and successful use of the recombinant chains. (D) reverses the role of the connecting peptide during normal maturation.

Key point: Distinguish expression, precursor processing and final protein assembly in a recombinant product.

Q10 Biology · hard

Ecology / An observed census identifies reproduction before an age-structured second interval

Answer: (B) b=1.50 and expected total 240.

Given: Only adults present at an interval's start reproduce; survival and maturation precede the next age census.

Formula/Principle: Keep births, surviving cohorts and migration separate before updating the age structure.

Step 1: Adults at census 1 are A1​=0.5(40)+0.75(80)+10−10=80.

Step 2: New juveniles are J1​=80b, so 80+80b=200⇒b=1.50,J1​=120.

Step 3: For the second interval, J2​=1.5(80)=120,A2​=0.5(120)+0.75(80)=120.

Step 4: N2​=J2​+A2​=240.

Why: The total count alone is insufficient for the next projection because juveniles and adults have different roles and survival. Births in one interval enlarge the next juvenile cohort but do not become same-interval breeders. Cancelling net migration does not justify omitting maturation or adult mortality. These are stipulated expected counts, not an assumption of logistic growth or a field estimate of carrying capacity.

Why not the others: (A) omits the 20 maturing juveniles when inferring b. (C) uses the 120 juveniles as if they were the current breeding adults in interval 2. (D) neither reproduces the observed census with the stated surviving adults nor updates its age composition.

Key point: Preserve cohort identity when moving from a population balance to a second projection.

Q11 Biology · medium

Genetics And Evolution / Common ancestry with ecological divergence contrasted with independent functional resemblance

Answer: (A) Adaptive radiation in the birds and convergence in the mammalian comparison.

Why: Diversification from one ancestral stock into different ecological roles is the defining pattern of adaptive radiation. Similar adaptive forms appearing independently in distant lineages instead support convergent evolution. Functional similarity alone cannot establish a recent common origin, and different functions can arise among close relatives. The supplied ancestry observations therefore determine how the morphological similarities and differences are interpreted.

Why not the others: (B) discards the one-lineage origin of the birds and invents a shared recent origin for the distant mammals. (C) makes an unsupported claim about directed within-individual mutation rather than population evolution. (D) equates matching function with identical ancestry.

Key point: Use the ancestry pattern to distinguish divergence into niches from independent resemblance.

Q12 Biology · easy

Human Physiology / Vital capacity excludes the residual compartment despite a maximal inspiration

Answer: (C) 3500 mL.

Given: TV=500 mL, IRV=2000 mL, ERV=1000 mL and RV=1200 mL.

Formula/Principle: Vital capacity is the volume between maximal inspiration and maximal expiration.

Step 1: VC=IRV+TV+ERV.

Step 2: VC=2000+500+1000=3500 mL.

Why: Residual volume stays in the lungs after the specified maximal expiration and is outside the requested moving volume. It contributes to total lung capacity, not to vital capacity. The calculation identifies the two endpoint states before combining the named volumes.

Why not the others: (A) includes residual volume and gives total lung capacity. (B) leaves out ordinary tidal volume. (D) adds residual volume to tidal volume while ignoring both reserves.

Key point: Define the starting and ending respiratory states before adding volume components.

Q13 Biology · medium

Human Physiology / An acute medullary signal and a fasting islet signal share an endpoint but not a source

Answer: (D) Adrenaline and alpha-cell glucagon.

Why: The adrenal medulla supplies catecholamines such as adrenaline in the acute stress response. Pancreatic alpha cells release glucagon, which helps raise available glucose during fasting, whereas beta-cell insulin generally promotes glucose uptake and storage. Similar effects on a measured glucose variable do not make the hormones identical or give them the same tissue source. Source, cell type and physiological trigger jointly identify the pair.

Why not the others: (A) assigns the medullary rapid signal to a cortical hormone and pairs fasting mobilisation with insulin. (B) retains adrenaline but gives insulin the wrong islet cell and action. (C) substitutes thyroid hormone for the medullary signal and places glucagon in beta cells.

Key point: Combine endocrine source, trigger and action rather than identifying a hormone from one endpoint alone.

Q14 Biology · medium

Cell: Structure And Functions / Vesicle-fusion blockade interrupts plant cytokinesis after successful nuclear separation

Answer: (B) A binucleate cell without the initial cell plate.

Why: In the depicted plant-cell cytokinesis route, vesicles fuse centrally to form the cell plate and associated new partition. Blocking their fusion prevents this cytoplasmic separation even though karyokinesis has already produced two daughter nuclei. No reversal of chromosome segregation is required for the cell to remain binucleate. The observed vesicle location identifies the relevant plant mechanism rather than an animal-type constricting furrow.

Why not the others: (A) substitutes a different cytokinesis mechanism and removes nuclei that the stem says are present. (C) invents nuclear fusion and a ploidy reduction with no stated cause. (D) assigns a backward DNA-synthesis requirement to a membrane-partitioning step.

Key point: Nuclear division and cytoplasmic partitioning are separable events with different cellular machinery.

Q15 Biology · hard

Reproduction / Complementary blastocyst-lineage defects separate fertilisation, implantation and embryo-proper development

Answer: (D) X separates attachment capacity from embryo formation; Y separates blastocyst formation from implantation.

Why: The trophoblast participates in attachment to the uterine lining and later maternal-fetal interactions, while the inner cell mass supplies the embryo proper. Losing the inner cell mass therefore does not logically erase an already formed trophoblast's initial adhesion capability, but it prevents normal embryo-proper development. Conversely, having an inner cell mass does not substitute for the specified trophoblast adhesion function. The stage chronology also matters: fertilisation and cleavage precede blastocyst attachment, so an implantation defect does not prove those earlier events never occurred. This deliberately limited model does not assert that a trophoblast alone forms every tissue of a complete placenta.

Why not the others: (A) ignores loss of the embryo-forming lineage and the specified adhesion defect. (B) confuses the attachment role of trophoblast with the embryo-proper role of inner cell mass. (C) infers failure of an earlier completed stage from a later functional defect.

Key point: Distinguish stage chronology from lineage-specific functions.

WORKED SOLUTIONS / C

Chemistry

Method, reasoning and common errors

Q16 Chemistry · medium

Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure / Opposite bonding effects of electron removal give equal final bond orders but new spin counts

Answer: (C) N2 weakens, O2 strengthens, and each ion has one unpaired electron.

Given: Removal occurs from a bonding orbital in N2 and an antibonding orbital in O2.

Formula/Principle: Bond order is (Nb​−Na​)/2; removing a bonding electron lowers it, while removing an antibonding electron raises it.

Step 1: Neutral N2 has bond order 3. Its ion has BO(NX2​X+)=3−1/2=2.5.

Step 2: Neutral O2 has bond order 2. Its ion has BO(OX2​X+)=2+1/2=2.5.

Step 3: The formerly paired N2 frontier orbital becomes singly occupied. Removing one of O2's two frontier electrons leaves one unpaired electron.

Why: Ionisation need not weaken every molecular bond; its effect depends on whether the removed electron supported or opposed bonding. Equal final bond orders do not mean equal changes from the neutral species. Magnetic behaviour must be counted from occupancy rather than inferred solely from the fact that an electron was removed.

Why not the others: (A) treats both removed electrons as antibonding and miscounts the remaining spins. (B) reverses the bonding roles and pairs odd-electron ions. (D) treats both removed electrons as bonding and ignores the changed frontier occupations.

Key point: Identify the removed orbital's bonding character before predicting ionisation effects.

Q17 Chemistry · hard

Coordination compounds / A spin measurement determines oxidation state before salt stoichiometry and anion naming

Answer: (A) K3[Fe(CN)6], potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III).

Given: The allowed oxidation states are +2 and +3; both octahedral candidates are low spin.

Formula/Principle: Use the magnetic moment to infer unpaired count, low-spin d occupancy to identify oxidation state, then balance ligand charge and apply anionic-complex naming.

Step 1: u(u+2)=3⇒u=1 for nonnegative integer u.

Step 2: Fe(II) is d6 and low-spin t2g6​, with zero unpaired electrons. Fe(III) is d5 and low-spin t2g5​, with one, so the metal is Fe(III).

Step 3: qcomplex​=+3+6(−1)=−3, requiring three potassium ions.

Step 4: Six cyanido ligands give hexacyanido; an anionic iron complex takes ferrate, followed by oxidation number III.

Why: A magnetic measurement supplies electron-configuration evidence rather than the oxidation number directly. Low-spin information makes the two permitted oxidation states distinguishable, and the resulting charge determines the salt stoichiometry. The ligand count is a coordination count, not the metal oxidation number.

Why not the others: (B) describes the diamagnetic low-spin Fe(II) candidate. (C) omits the anionic metal-name form. (D) substitutes the ligand count six for the inferred oxidation state three.

Key point: Connect magnetic occupancy, ionic charge and nomenclature as separate deductions.

Q18 Chemistry · medium

The d- & f-block elements / An acid-driven colour change is separated from a subsequent chromium reduction

Answer: (D) The first preserves +6; the second accepts six electrons.

Given: CrOX4​X2− interconverts with CrX2​OX7​X2−, then Cr(III) forms.

Formula/Principle: Determine chromium oxidation states from oxygen and ion charge before deciding whether a colour change is redox.

Step 1: In chromate, x+4(−2)=−2⇒x=+6.

Step 2: In dichromate, 2x+7(−2)=−2⇒x=+6.

Step 3: Reduction of both chromium atoms from +6 to +3 accepts 2(6−3)=6 electrons.

Why: Acidification changes the equilibrium distribution of chromium(VI) oxoanions and their colour, but it does not change the chromium oxidation number. The later reduction does change that number and requires electron uptake. Visible colour alone therefore cannot classify a reaction as oxidation or reduction.

Why not the others: (A) equates a spectral change with redox regardless of oxidation states. (B) assigns the later reduced state to the acid-base interconversion. (C) invents electron loss in the first step and omits electron gain in the second.

Key point: Track oxidation numbers independently of colour when identifying a redox change.

Q19 Chemistry · easy

Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties / Different radius definitions prevent an unsupported cross-definition periodic trend

Answer: (B) Different operational definitions are being compared.

Why: A covalent radius is associated with bonded-atom separation, whereas a van der Waals radius is obtained from nonbonded contacts. Noble-gas entries commonly use the latter because ordinary covalent-bond data are not comparable to the bonded-atom data used for many other elements. The numerical difference is real for those definitions, but it cannot by itself establish the stated change in one common radius measure or its cause.

Why not the others: (A) puts adjacent period-3 atoms in different principal shells. (C) reverses their proton-number order. (D) denies the meaning of a positive nonbonded-contact distance rather than identifying the definition mismatch.

Key point: Check how a periodic-property measurement is defined before comparing its numbers.

Q20 Chemistry · medium

Structure of the Atom / Specified hydrogen-like transitions coincide after simultaneous level and charge scaling

Answer: (C) Three distinct photon energies.

Given: H has Z=1 and He+ has Z=2; every selected He+ level is twice the corresponding H level.

Formula/Principle: A transition energy is the difference between its two level energies, and coincident differences count only once.

Step 1: For a He+ level 2n, E2n​=−E0​(2n)222​=−E0​/n2, the same energy as H level n.

Step 2: The paired transitions therefore coincide: 6 to 4 with 3 to 2; 6 to 2 with 3 to 1; and 4 to 2 with 2 to 1.

Step 3: The three distinct positive differences are 365E0​​,98E0​​,43E0​​.

Why: Counting named transitions is different from counting observed photon-energy values. Nuclear-charge scaling exactly compensates for the doubled level labels in the specified pairs. The question restricts the transition set; it does not assert that an actual unrestricted He+ cascade lacks other lines.

Why not the others: (A) counts each species' coincident line separately. (B) merges only two pairs and misses the full level scaling. (D) incorrectly identifies two of the three unequal energy gaps as the same.

Key point: Compare energy differences after nuclear-charge scaling before counting distinct spectral lines.

Q21 Chemistry · medium

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Hydration stoichiometry and a later aliquot require separate mole accounts

Answer: (A) x=5 and 5.00×10−4 mol.

Given: Anhydrous residue is 0.500−0.180=0.320 g; all of it enters the stated solution.

Formula/Principle: Infer hydrate stoichiometry from water-to-salt mole ratio, then use the aliquot fraction of a homogeneous solution.

Step 1: nsalt​=0.320/160=0.00200 mol,nwater​=0.180/18.0=0.0100 mol.

Step 2: x=nwater​/nsalt​=5.

Step 3: n25​=0.00200(25.0/100.0)=5.00×10−4 mol.

Why: The starting mass includes water, so it cannot be divided directly by the anhydrous molar mass to count salt units. Heating separates the two mass contributions under the explicit no-decomposition assumption. Dilution changes concentration but conserves the salt amount, and a quarter-volume aliquot contains a quarter of those units.

Why not the others: (B) reports the whole solution's amount for the aliquot. (C) uses the wrong water-to-salt mole ratio despite the correct aliquot amount. (D) miscounts both hydrate water and the sampled fraction.

Key point: Separate crystallisation water from anhydrous formula units before handling solution aliquots.

Q22 Chemistry · medium

Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques / Two eluents change an Rf value without proving chemical reaction or yield

Answer: (D) Rf increases from 0.20 to 0.60 without proving conversion.

Given: Distances are measured from each plate's own baseline to its spot and solvent front.

Formula/Principle: Rf​=dspot​/dfront​ for the specified stationary and mobile phases.

Step 1: Rf,X​=2.0/10.0=0.20.

Step 2: Rf,Y​=4.8/8.0=0.60.

Why: Migration reflects the compound's relative interactions with the stationary phase and the particular eluent. Changing the mobile phase can therefore change Rf for the same compound. Neither spot travel nor its ratio to the solvent front is a chemical yield measurement, and the data alone do not demonstrate a new covalent species.

Why not the others: (A) miscalculates the second ratio and gives it a reaction-yield meaning. (B) uses a complementary or incorrect distance for X and invents decomposition. (C) ignores dependence on the chromatographic conditions.

Key point: A chromatographic migration ratio is condition-dependent evidence, not an intrinsic reaction-progress meter.

Q23 Chemistry · medium

Hydrocarbons / The same internal alkyne follows stereoselective reduction or carbonyl-forming hydration

Answer: (C) cis-But-2-ene and butan-2-one.

Why: Controlled Lindlar hydrogenation adds hydrogen to an alkyne while stopping at the alkene, with the cis product from this internal alkyne. Hydration first gives an enol that converts to the more stable carbonyl form, here butan-2-one. But-2-yne is symmetric, so the hydration orientations do not create different constitutional ketones. Both routes retain all four carbons but lead to different functional groups.

Why not the others: (A) assigns the trans-selective outcome of a different reduction route to Lindlar conditions. (B) changes an internal-alkyne hydration product into an aldehyde. (D) over-reduces the first aliquot and treats the hydration enol route as ordinary ketone reduction.

Key point: Distinguish selective alkyne reduction from hydration followed by enol-carbonyl conversion.

Q24 Chemistry · easy

Haloalkanes and haloarenes / Geminal and vicinal starting connectivity converge after two valid elimination stages

Answer: (B) P geminal, Q vicinal, and ethyne.

Why: In P both halogens are attached to one carbon, whereas in Q they are on adjacent carbons. Those arrangements define geminal and vicinal dihalides, respectively. Removing two HBr units under the stated sufficiently strong conditions creates a carbon-carbon triple bond in either two-carbon substrate. The explicit second-stage condition avoids assuming an ordinary mild base always completes elimination from a vinyl halide.

Why not the others: (A) reverses the two classifications and removes only one degree of unsaturation. (C) keeps the classifications but replaces elimination by reduction to a saturated hydrocarbon. (D) reverses the classifications and stops at the first elimination product.

Key point: Classify halogen positions separately from how far a staged elimination proceeds.

Q25 Chemistry · medium

Alcohols, phenols, and ethers / A phenol control prevents misclassifying every negative Lucas test as a primary alcohol

Answer: (D) The test response must be interpreted within the functional-group class.

Why: The tertiary aliphatic alcohol readily undergoes the substitution that produces turbidity under Lucas conditions. In phenol the OH is attached directly to an aromatic carbon; its bonding and substitution behaviour differ from the aliphatic carbinol systems used for the usual primary-secondary-tertiary Lucas comparison. Failure to give that response therefore does not assign phenol to the primary-alcohol category. A negative result narrows an interpretation only after the sample's functional-group context is checked.

Why not the others: (A) contradicts the known OH in phenol. (B) invents a tertiary alkyl carbocation at an aromatic carbon and an unmeasured optical concealment. (C) applies the aliphatic carbon-substitution classification to the wrong carbon type.

Key point: Do not extend a diagnostic-test classification beyond the functional groups for which it is defined.

Q26 Chemistry · medium

Biomolecules / Selective peptide hydrolysis preserves a disulfide-linked pair of residues as one molecule

Answer: (A) Three water molecules and three separate product molecules.

Given: Four residues form one linear peptide backbone; a side-chain S-S connection joins the two terminal cysteine residues.

Formula/Principle: Count peptide bonds for hydrolysis, then count connected covalent products after those bonds alone are removed.

Step 1: A linear four-residue backbone has Npeptide​=4−1=3 peptide bonds, consuming three water molecules.

Step 2: Glycine and alanine each become one separate molecule. The two cysteine-derived residues remain connected to one another through S-S, giving one cystine molecule.

Step 3: Nproducts​=1+1+1=3.

Why: The side-chain crosslink does not add a peptide bond, but it does keep two residues in one covalent product after the backbone is hydrolysed. Counting residues alone would correctly describe four amino-acid units but incorrectly describe four separate molecules. The treatment's bond selectivity is essential to this distinction.

Why not the others: (B) silently reduces or cleaves the retained disulfide bond. (C) counts the S-S link as another water-consuming peptide hydrolysis. (D) undercounts the linear backbone's three peptide connections.

Key point: Distinguish bond count from connected-product count when a peptide has a nonpeptide crosslink.

Q27 Chemistry · medium

Equilibrium / Equal-pH buffers respond in different equilibrium regimes to the same acid dose

Answer: (C) 2.00 and 9+log(2/3).

Given: Equal initial ratios give equal initial pH, but X contains one-tenth the buffer amount.

Formula/Principle: Neutralise B first; only a solution retaining both B and BH+ can use the buffer relation pH=14−pKb​+log(nB​/nBH+​).

Step 1: In X all 0.0100 mol B is protonated. Excess strong acid is 0.0200−0.0100=0.0100 mol,[H+]≃0.0100 M,pHX​=2.00.

Step 2: In Y, nB​=0.100−0.0200=0.0800,nBH+​=0.100+0.0200=0.120 mol.

Step 3: pHY​=9.00+log(0.0800/0.120)=9+log(2/3)≈8.82.

Why: Initial pH constrains a ratio, not the total amount available to absorb acid. The same dose exhausts X's base and leaves a strong-acid excess, while Y remains a buffer. BH+ has Ka=10^-9, so its additional dissociation in X is negligible beside the supplied 0.0100 M strong acid.

Why not the others: (A) inverts Y's surviving base-to-acid ratio. (B) treats equal initial pH as unlimited resistance to added acid. (D) uses all added HCl rather than the excess after neutralisation in X.

Key point: Buffer capacity and buffer pH are different properties; change the model when one partner is exhausted.

Q28 Chemistry · medium

Solutions / Measured liquid and vapour compositions determine a partial-vaporisation amount by conservation

Answer: (D) One-third of the moles are vapour, which is enriched in A.

Given: Feed fraction z=0.40, liquid fraction x=0.30, vapour fraction y=0.60.

Formula/Principle: Conserve total moles and the moles of A across the two phases.

Step 1: Let v be the fraction of feed moles in vapour, leaving 1-v in liquid.

Step 2: A balance gives 0.40=0.30(1−v)+0.60v⇒0.10=0.30v⇒v=1/3.

Step 3: Since 0.60>0.40>0.30, vapour is enriched and liquid depleted in A relative to the original feed.

Why: A phase composition is not the fraction of feed that entered that phase. The two composition measurements must be combined with conservation of A to infer phase amounts. The calculation does not assume equal liquid and vapour quantities or identify either phase composition with the original mixture.

Why not the others: (A) reports the fraction remaining liquid as the vapour fraction. (B) averages the two compositions as if phase amounts had to be equal. (C) obtains the fraction but reverses the enrichment comparison.

Key point: Use component balance to separate phase amounts from phase compositions.

Q29 Chemistry · hard

Electrochemistry / Free-ion complexation and reaction scaling separate intensive voltage from extensive Gibbs change

Answer: (A) 0.1816 V and Gibbs-change ratio 2.

Given: Pure solid activities are one; the original electron count is two and Nernst activities are those of participating free ions.

Formula/Principle: Scaling a reaction scales both its electron count and the logarithm of its quotient; cell potential is intensive, while ΔG=−nFE follows the written reaction amount.

Step 1: Q=a(BX2+)a(AX2+)​=10−2/10−6=104.

Step 2: For the original equation, E=0.3000−(0.0592/2)(4)=0.1816 V.

Step 3: The doubled equation has n′=4 and Q′=Q2=108, giving E′=0.3000−(0.0592/4)(8)=0.1816 V.

Step 4: ΔGΔG′​=−2FE−4FE′​=2.

Why: Complexed B is not interchangeable with the explicitly participating free ion in the quotient. Rewriting a balanced equation does not alter the physical voltage, because the simultaneous quotient and electron-count changes cancel. Q59 Physics · medium

Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter / Acceleration followed by partial retardation before a wavelength ratio

Answer: (A) 2/√3.

Given: The second potential removes 100 eV from the 400 eV kinetic energy.

Formula/Principle: λ=h/2mK​; successive energy changes must be combined with their signs.

Step 1: Ki​=400 eV and Kf​=400−100=300 eV, positive as required for transmission.

Worked derivation: λf​/λi​=Ki​/Kf​​=400/300​=2/3​.

Why: Retardation lowers momentum, increasing wavelength. The final energy is not simply the energy corresponding to the retarding voltage.

Why not the others: (B) It treats 100 eV as the final energy and reverses the ratio. (C) It inverts the wavelength ratio. (D) It makes wavelength inversely proportional to energy instead of its square root.

Key point: Sum signed kinetic-energy changes before converting to matter wavelength.

Q60 Physics · easy

Semiconductor Electronics / Battery reversal selects unequal antiparallel diode paths

Answer: (B) 60 mA then 30 mA.

Given: An ideal forward diode is a short and a reverse diode an open circuit.

Formula/Principle: Select the conducting path for each polarity and apply Ohm's law only to that path.

Step 1: Left positive forward-biases the 100 ohm branch: I1​=6/100=0.060 A.

Step 2: Right positive forward-biases the opposite 200 ohm branch: I2​=6/200=0.030 A.

Worked derivation: (∣I1​∣,∣I2​∣)=(60,30) mA.

Why: Reversing the battery swaps which branch is closed; both branches are never simultaneously conducting in this ideal DC model.

Why not the others: (A) It reverses the two bias conditions. (C) It adds currents from a blocked branch. (D) Each polarity has one forward path.

Key point: Establish diode state before reducing the circuit.
